html:
Pearl hunting is the gathering of pearls and pearl shell from oysters, for most of history by divers holding their breath. Natural pearls were among the costliest goods of the ancient and medieval world.

The Persian Gulf was the greatest source for thousands of years, above all the banks off Bahrain and the Arab coast. Each summer fleets of boats went out for the diving season. Divers with nose clips and a stone to sink them went down again and again, and were hauled up by rope. Merchants advanced money, and many divers were trapped in debt; some were enslaved Africans. The trade fed towns such as Kuwait and the coast of the Trucial States, now the United Arab Emirates. Other pearl coasts lay between India and Sri Lanka, in the Red Sea, and off Venezuela and Panama, where the Spanish forced Native and African divers to work.

In northwest Australia from the 1860s, pearling boats hunted shell for buttons and forced Aboriginal people such as the Jabirr Jabirr and Djugun to dive. In the 1920s and 1930s Japanese cultured pearls, perfected by Kokichi Mikimoto, together with the Great Depression ruined the Gulf trade, just before oil changed the region.
